etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English cool, from Old English cōl (“cool, cold, tranquil, calm”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōl(ī), from Proto-Germanic *kōlaz, *kōluz (“cool”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian köil (“cool”), West Frisian koel (“cool”), Dutch koel (“cool”), Limburgish kool (“cool”), German Low German köhl (“cool”), German kühl (“cool”). Related to cold.

definitions.definition: Of a mildly low temperature.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter VIII, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: The day was cool and snappy for August, and the Rise all green with a lavish nature. Now we plunged into a deep shade with the boughs lacing each other overhead, and crossed dainty, rustic bridges over the cold trout-streams, the boards giving back the clatter of our horses' feet: […] .

definitions.definition: Allowing or suggesting heat relief.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 2, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: Now that she had rested and had fed from the luncheon tray Mrs. Broome had just removed, she had reverted to her normal gaiety.  She looked cool in a grey tailored cotton dress with a terracotta scarf and shoes and her hair a black silk helmet.

definitions.definition: Of a color, in the range of violet to green.
(of a person) Not showing emotion; calm and in control of oneself.
Unenthusiastic, lukewarm, skeptical.
Calmly audacious.

quote.citation: 1868, Louisa M[ay] Alcott, chapter 13, in Little Women: […], part first, Boston, Mass.: Roberts Brothers, published 1869, →OCLC:
quote.text: "Well, that's cool," said Laurie to himself, "to have a picnic and never ask me!"

quote.citation: 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne, “V. Hester at her Needle”, in The Scarlet Letter‎[1]:
quote.text: Its cool stare of familiarity was intolerable.

definitions.definition: Applied facetiously to a sum of money, commonly as if to give emphasis to the largeness of the amount.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London: A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Who will lend me a cool hundred.

quote.citation: 1860 December – 1861 August, Charles Dickens, chapter XVIII, in Great Expectations […], volume III, London: Chapman and Hall, […], published October 1861, →OCLC, page 303:
quote.text: But she had wrote out a little coddleshell in her own hand a day or two afore the accident, leaving a cool four thousand to Mr. Matthew Pocket.
You remember Bulger, don't you? You lost a cool hundred to him one night here over the cards, eh?

quote.citation: 1944 November 28, Irving Brecher and Fred F. Finklehoffe, Meet Me in St. Louis, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer:
quote.text: My father was talking to the World's Fair Commission yesterday, and they estimate it's going to cost a cool fifty million.

definitions.definition: (informal, of a person) Knowing what to do and how to behave; behaving with effortless and enviable style and panache; considered popular by others.

quote.citation: 2017 December 27, “The Guardian view on Prince Harry: the monarchy’s best insurance policy”, in the Guardian‎[2]:
quote.text: He managed to conduct interviews with the least cool global figure – his father, Prince Charles – and the most cool, Barack Obama, in a way that allowed them both to look as good as they could.

definitions.definition: (informal, originally African-American Vernacular) Fashionable; trendy and hip.

quote.citation: 2008, Lou Schuler, "Foreward", in Nate Green, Built for Show, page xii
quote.text: The fact that I was middle-aged, bald, married, and raising girls instead of chasing them didn't really bother me. Muscles are cool at any age.

definitions.definition: (informal) All right; acceptable.

quote.citation: 1962, “Monster Mash”, Bobby "Boris" Pickett, Lenny Capizzi (lyrics), performed by Bobby (Boris) Pickett and The Crypt-Kickers:
quote.text: Now everything's cool, Drac's a part of the band / And my Monster Mash is the hit of the land / For you, the living, this Mash was meant too / When you get to my door, tell them Boris sent you.

definitions.definition: (informal) Very interesting or exciting.
(informal) Followed by with, able to tolerate.
(informal) Of a pair of people, Having good relations.
A moderate or refreshing state of cold; moderate temperature of the air between hot and cold; coolness.
A calm temperament.
The property of being cool, popular or in fashion.

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English colen, from Old English cōlian (“to cool, grow cold, be cold”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlēn (“to become cold”), from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to freeze”).

Cognate with Dutch koelen (“to cool”), German kühlen (“to cool”), Swedish kyla (“to cool, refrigerate”). Also partially from Middle English kelen, from Old English cēlan (“to cool, be cold, become cold”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōlijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōlijaną (“to cool”), altered to resemble the adjective cool. See keel.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, literally) To lose heat, to get colder.
(transitive, literally) To make cooler, less warm.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 16:24:
quote.text: Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively) To become less intense, e.g. less amicable or passionate.
(transitive, figuratively) To make less intense, e.g. less amicable or passionate.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: We have reason to cool our raging motions, our carnal stings, our unbitted lusts.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang, dated) To kill, murder.

quote.text: Maybe he would die. That would mean I had murdered him. I smiled, trying the idea on for size. One of the things that always had cheesed me a little was that I had no kills to my credit. I'd been in plenty of rumbles, but somehow, I'd never cooled anyone. Well maybe now I had my first one. I couldn't feel very proud of skulling an old man, but at least I could say that I'd scored. That was a big kick.

quote.citation: 1967, Piri Thomas, Down These Mean Streets, New York, N.Y.: Alfred A. Knopf, page 31:
quote.text: Big-mouth got up as fast as he could, and I was thinking how much heart he had. But I ran toward him like my life depended on it; I wanted to cool him.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, African-American Vernacular, slang) To relax, hang out.

quote.text: Seen my homeboys coolin' way way out / Told 'em bout my mornin' cold bugged' em out

quote.citation: 2000, Paul Beatty, Tuff: A Novel, New York, N.Y.: Anchor Books, published 2001, →ISBN, page 223:
'1997, Courttia Newland, The Scholar: A West Side Story, London: Abacus, →ISBN, page 207:
quote.text: Asbestos? Raa, dat's a dangerous t'ing boy, dat ain't good. You know what though, you guys should min' yourselves walkin' street star, dere's bere nutters about. I know you're in a crew but boy can't you jus' cool at someone's house?'
